St. Johnsbury.metaDescription: Raccoons, bats, squirrels, and skunks in St. Johnsbury, VT — historic in-town homes where the Passumpsic and Moose rivers meet. Same-day service — call us today.
St. Johnsbury.housing_era: The Northeast Kingdom's hub, with grand Victorian homes on the hill streets, older mill and railroad-era housing along Railroad Street and the rivers, and farmhouses spreading toward Danville, Barnet, and Waterford.
St. Johnsbury.geographic_features: Passumpsic River (flows through town to the Connecticut River), Moose River (joins the Passumpsic in town), Sleepers River (tributary crossing the western side of town), Connecticut River (a short drive east, forming the New Hampshire border)

St. Johnsbury.wildlife_intro:
St. Johnsbury's older housing and three rivers make it the Kingdom's busiest small-town wildlife market. Bats colony in the tall attics of Victorian homes, raccoons and squirrels work the hill neighborhoods and river flats, and skunks are a spring staple under porches across town. Out on the edges, farm calls involve raccoons in barns, woodchucks in the fields, and the occasional fisher troubling a chicken coop.

Winters here are among the coldest in Vermont, so mice and squirrels push inside hard in October and November, and a house that is not proofed by snow will host them until spring. Mud season brings out skunks and denning raccoons, and summer bat work is exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, proofing in winter, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Our crew plans every St. Johnsbury job around that calendar.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your farmhouse, barn, or camp in St. Johnsbury, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: Do fishers really cause problems around St. Johnsbury?
faqs.a: They can on rural properties. Fishers are strong forest predators that will raid chicken coops and occasionally take outdoor cats, and they are common in the Kingdom woods. Our crew can remove a problem fisher lawfully — compensated trapping requires a valid Vermont trapping license — and help you secure coops and outbuildings so the loss does not repeat.

Lyndon.wildlife_intro:
Lyndon's calls split between Lyndonville's older village homes — attic bats, chimney raccoons, and squirrels in the big street maples — and the farms and camps out along the Passumpsic. Beavers are a recurring rural problem here, damming culverts and flooding hay land and camp roads, and raccoons and skunks work the barns and feed storage. Red squirrels and mice are constant in the wooded camps toward Burke Mountain.

Long Kingdom winters mean fall proofing is the most valuable job we do in Lyndon, and beaver work often peaks in spring and fall when dams raise water where nobody wants it. Summer bat colonies in village homes are handled by exclusion only, timed for spring or late August through November, with winter reserved for proofing cold, empty attics. If water is rising behind a new dam on your land, call us and our crew will walk through the lawful options.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: What can be done about beavers flooding my Lyndon driveway or field?
faqs.a: Beaver problems are solved case by case — sometimes a pond-leveling pipe keeps water at a height everyone can live with, and sometimes the animals have to be trapped out by someone holding a valid Vermont trapping license. Our crew will look at the site, explain which route fits, and handle the work. Relocating furbearers is prohibited in Vermont, so we will not promise that.

Hardwick.wildlife_intro:
Hardwick's wildlife is farm and village work in equal measure. Raccoons get into barns, sweet corn, and chicken coops, bats roost in the village's older homes and big farm barns, and woodchucks dig under sheds and along garden edges all over town. Squirrels — gray in the village, red in the woods — are the most common attic call, and beavers occasionally back water up into low fields along the Lamoille and its brooks.

Mud season in Hardwick brings skunks out from under porches and raccoons looking for den sites, while fall sends rodents and squirrels into houses ahead of a long winter. Bat jobs follow Vermont Fish and Wildlife best practice: exclusion with one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, full proofing from December through March, and no colony work while pups are flightless. Our crew will tell you plainly which window your job falls in when you call.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: Why do I hear scratching in my Hardwick walls every winter?
faqs.a: Most often it is mice or a red or gray squirrel using a wall void or attic corner for winter shelter, entering through a small roofline or foundation gap. Our crew finds the entry, removes the animals, and seals the opening with chew-proof material. Winter is actually a good time for that proofing work, before spring litters arrive.

Danville.wildlife_intro:
Danville's calls are classic hill-farm work: bats in farmhouse attics and barns, raccoons in feed rooms and chimneys, squirrels in the village homes around the green, and woodchucks under every kind of outbuilding. Around Joe's Pond, seasonal camps add their own pattern — mice and red squirrels over the winter, bats in the summer, and beavers and muskrats working the shoreline and the pond's outlet brooks.

A camp closed in September can hold a winter of mouse damage by May, so our crew does a lot of fall proofing and spring clean-out work around the pond. Bat exclusion on both camps and farmhouses is timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors, and winter is for sealing empty buildings, never for trapping a colony inside. Call us in the fall and we will close your place up before the snow flies.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Danville, VT?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your farmhouse, barn, or camp in Danville, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: What is the best time to proof a Joe's Pond camp against mice and squirrels?
faqs.a: Late summer and early fall, while you are still visiting and can confirm nothing is living inside. Our crew seals foundation gaps, screens vents, and closes roofline openings with chew-proof material, then checks traps and signs at opening. A camp proofed in September is a far easier opening in May.

Barnet.wildlife_intro:
Barnet stretches from Connecticut River intervale farms up through forested hills to Harvey Lake, and each band has its animals. Raccoons and skunks work the river farms and village homes, beavers dam the valley brooks and flood roads and fields, and bats roost in farmhouse attics and lake camps alike. Opossums are established in the Connecticut River valley, so Barnet is one of the Kingdom towns where they do turn up, usually under decks and in outbuildings.

Spring on the river means denning raccoons and skunks, summer means bat colonies in warm attics, and fall means mice and squirrels looking for winter quarters in both farmhouses and camps. Bat exclusion follows the seasonal rule — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, proofing in winter, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Our crew covers the whole town, from McIndoe Falls up to the lake, so call us wherever you are.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Barnet, VT?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your farmhouse, barn, or camp in Barnet, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: Are opossums really found in Barnet? I thought they were not in the Northeast Kingdom.
faqs.a: They are scarce across most of the Kingdom, but they are established in the Connecticut River valley, and Barnet sits right on the river. A mild-winter valley corridor lets them persist here at the edge of their Vermont range. If one moves under your deck or into an outbuilding, our crew can remove it and close the access.
